trials.hypothesis: Pour les grandes entrées, 256 threads accumulant 8 valeurs coalescées chacun devraient réduire le nombre de lancements de quatre réductions successives plus une copie à deux kernels, avec seulement un partiel écrit par CTA. Cette proposition teste la variante personnalisée warp/shuffle via warpReduceSum; une variante jumelle CUB BlockReduce devra être mesurée séparément pour comparer les primitives. Les petits n passent par un kernel direct (n=1 conserve la copie existante). Aucun gain n'est présumé avant mesure.

Réduction intra-bloc personnalisée par warpReduceSum et une synchronisation bloc pour agréger les sommes de warps.
Ajout d'un chemin direct à un kernel pour n <= 2048 et conservation de la copie device-to-device pour n == 1.
Calcul du nombre de partiels sans addition susceptible de déborder; chaque lecture d'entrée ou de partiel est bornée et chaque emplacement scratch lu est écrit durant l'appel.

Each CTA computes grid-stride 64-bit partial sums, the grid synchronizes, and CTA 0 writes the result. Runtime capability, occupancy, and launch checks gate this route; global synchronization and setup overhead may still erase any benefit, so the controller must measure it.

retained: Add a grid-stride cooperative reduction kernel that writes 64-bit CTA partials, performs a Cooperative Groups grid sync, and lets CTA 0 produce out.
Query runtime cooperative-launch support and kernel occupancy; cap the grid at activeBlocksPerSM times multiprocessor count and fall back if the cooperative launch is unavailable or rejected.
Keep the existing multistage reduction and copy path for small inputs and as the correctness fallback.

La remise à zéro de out dans le flux par défaut précède les atomiques; leur contention reste un compromis à mesurer face à l'alternative int64 en scratch avec conversion finale.

Réinitialiser explicitement out via cudaMemsetAsync dans le flux par défaut puis atomically accumuler chaque partiel après conversion unsigned modulo 2^32.
Laisser scratch inutilisé afin de tester la variante d'accumulation directe dans out, sans allocation supplémentaire ni kernel de finalisation.

trials.hypothesis: Adapter les tuiles de 2048 à 4096 valeurs dans la réduction hiérarchique mesurée de T1 peut diviser par deux le nombre de partiels et le travail du dernier kernel. La réduction finale élargie à 64 bits protège les sommes intermédiaires, puisque seul le résultat réel est garanti int32. Le gain de performance n’est pas établi avant mesure.

Passer le nombre d’éléments traités par thread de 8 à 16 : 256 threads forment désormais une tuile de 4096 valeurs, réduisant le nombre de partiels pour les grandes entrées.
Effectuer l’accumulation finale en long long et convertir le résultat en int32 une fois, afin de préserver l’exactitude lorsque les sommes intermédiaires dépassent int32.

Keep the 128-thread CTA, input tile size, recursive launch sequence, partial counts, and output copy unchanged.

Mixed words still fall back to the existing bounded scalar parser, so inputs with frequent non-ASCII bytes may see no benefit or regress from the extra load and branch. No speedup is presumed. The catalog has 26 distinct programs in 26 trials with no repeats; the best reported candidate is 40.76 µs, while the recent per-lead lookup measured 49.16 µs, so this tests a different scalar fast path rather than assuming a table/state-machine approach helps.

retained: Before bytewise scanning, inspect only complete eight-byte words copied through memcpy and skip a word only when its high-bit mask is zero.
For mixed words and short tails, retain bytewise ASCII scanning followed by bounded scalar UTF-8 sequence validation.

Preserve rejection of overlong encodings, surrogate encodings, illegal leads, out-of-range code points, and truncated sequences; preserve the ABI, complete uint32 output, read-only input, and serial execution.

trials.hypothesis: The selected 64-byte hybrid parent averaged 49.08 μs, while the best reported full-SIMD candidate averaged 13.38 μs. This separate SSE2 full-SIMD implementation tests whether byte-class masks, continuation relationships, and restricted second-byte checks can avoid scalar decoding on mixed blocks. SIMD comparison overhead or the scalar suffix may offset that benefit; no speedup is presumed.

retained: Replace the parent's 64-byte hybrid path with a separate 16-byte SSE2 full-SIMD validator; do not combine the two approaches.
Classify ASCII, continuation bytes, and legal 2-, 3-, and 4-byte leaders with SSE2 comparisons; reject bytes outside those classes.
Build continuation expectations from the leader masks, carry expected continuations across vectors, and compare them with the observed continuation mask.
Use a following in-bounds vector to check the restricted second-byte ranges for E0, ED, F0, and F4.
Leave a scalar suffix with a bounded overlap so sequences crossing the SIMD boundary and all remaining tail bytes are checked by the strict decoder.
Preserve the run ABI, full uint32_t result, input immutability, and serial execution; perform no load beyond n.

trials.hypothesis: A table-free scalar state machine tracking pending continuation bytes and the allowed range for the next byte may avoid per-code-point continuation lookahead, but adds state checks and range tests on continuation bytes. Retaining the bounds-checked ASCII word skip isolates this control-flow trade-off. Prior measurements show the byte-class DFA at 113.39 µs and the best reported direct scalar candidate at 40.76 µs; these results motivate testing branch-only state tracking but do not predict a speedup.

retained: Replace lead-specific multi-byte parsing with a scalar state machine that tracks the number of remaining continuation bytes and bounds for the next byte.
Preserve strict rejection of overlong encodings, surrogate encodings, illegal leads, values above U+10FFFF, invalid continuations, and incomplete sequences.
Retain the bounds-checked scalar 64-bit ASCII-word scan; no SIMD, input writes, ABI changes, or thread-budget changes.

trials.hypothesis: The selected full-SIMD parent averaged 27.02 μs; the best reported full-SIMD candidate averaged 13.38 μs. Earlier hybrid variants were correct but slower (about 46.94–56.77 μs). This candidate tests whether scanning 256-byte blocks with an SSE2 all-ASCII detector reduces block overhead enough to make the hybrid alternative more competitive. Mixed blocks still require strict scalar decoding, including sequences crossing the block boundary, so no speedup is presumed.

retained: Replace the full-SIMD loop with a separate hybrid path; use 256-byte blocks as the ASCII-skip unit.
For each complete block, OR-reduce sixteen in-bounds unaligned SSE2 loads and use the movemask to skip the block only when every byte is ASCII.
For a mixed block, strictly decode code points whose starts are before the block end, allowing a sequence to cross that boundary while checking against the full input length.
Use the same bounded strict decoder for the remaining tail, rejecting malformed continuations, overlong forms, surrogates, out-of-range values, and truncations.
Preserve the run ABI, full uint32_t output, input immutability, and serial execution; perform no load beyond n.

trials.hypothesis: Replacing per-byte pending-continuation state with sequence-local scalar decoding may reduce outer-loop state and special-case bounds handling. It instead adds a variable continuation loop, shifts, and post-decode scalar checks, so it may be slower than the best direct scalar parser; the unchanged repeated measurements must decide.

retained: Replace scan-wide pending-continuation state with lead dispatch and a per-sequence continuation loop that reconstructs the codepoint.
Check the complete continuation count before reading, then reject overlong encodings, surrogate codepoints, and values above U+10FFFF with generic scalar checks.
Retain the bounded ASCII-run scan, serial execution, read-only input, existing ABI, and complete uint32 output; introduce no SIMD or lookup table.

trials.hypothesis: The selected hybrid parent measured 52.51 μs; the prior 256-byte SSE2 hybrid measured 48.81 μs, while prior full-SIMD trials measured 17.76 μs and 13.38 μs. This standalone 16-byte SSE2 validator tests whether vector byte classification and continuation masks avoid the hybrid path's scalar fallback cost. It carries continuation expectations across blocks and uses the strict scalar decoder for the bounded tail. These historical measurements do not establish a speedup for this candidate or characterize every input mix.

retained: Replace the hybrid ASCII-skip loop with an independent SSE2 validator that classifies each complete 16-byte vector as ASCII, continuation, or a valid 2-, 3-, or 4-byte leader.
Build continuation expectations from leader masks and carry expected continuation bits across vectors; reject invalid byte classes and mismatched continuation positions.
Check the restricted second-byte ranges for E0, ED, F0, and F4 with SSE2 comparisons, handling the final vector lane with a bounded scalar check.
Consume any continuation bytes carried into the scalar tail, then validate remaining bytes with the existing strict bounds-checked scalar decoder.
Preserve the run ABI, uint32 output, input immutability, serial execution, and no-read-past-n behavior.

trials.hypothesis: A bounds-checked 8-byte high-bit scan can skip ASCII words, and a nonzero high-bit mask can locate the first non-ASCII byte even in a mixed word, avoiding byte-at-a-time ASCII checks before decoding. The added load, mask and bit scan may outweigh that saving. A prior all-ASCII-only word skip measured 58.21 µs versus the 49.60 µs baseline; the best reported direct scalar parser measured 40.76 µs. This is a distinct scalar prefix-scan variant, not SIMD, and no speedup is presumed.

retained: Replace byte-at-a-time ASCII prefix scanning with bounded memcpy loads of complete uint64_t words and a high-bit mask.

When a word contains non-ASCII, use a guarded scalar bit scan to advance to its first high-bit byte on little-endian GCC/Clang, with a byte-scan fallback; retain the existing sequence decoder and Unicode validity checks.
Preserve the ABI, complete uint32_t output, read-only input, bounded access, and serial execution.

trials.hypothesis: A standalone 16-byte SSE2 validator may improve on the selected 64-byte hybrid by checking byte classes, continuation relationships, and restricted second-byte ranges in vectors, carrying continuation expectations across vectors, and validating an overlapped suffix with the strict scalar decoder. Previous full-SIMD measurements include 13.38 μs, versus 49.08 μs for the selected hybrid, but this candidate's speed is unknown and the comparison is not a guarantee.

retained: Replaced the selected 64-byte ASCII-detection hybrid with an independent SSE2 full validator processing 16-byte vectors.
Classified ASCII, continuation, and legal 2-, 3-, and 4-byte leader lanes; rejected unclassified bytes and compared expected continuation masks with observed masks.
Carried continuation expectations across vector boundaries and checked E0, ED, F0, and F4 second-byte restrictions using an in-bounds overlapping load.
Used the strict scalar decoder on a suffix overlapped by up to three bytes, so boundary-crossing sequences and tails are validated without reads beyond n.
Preserved the run ABI, full uint32_t output, input immutability, and serial execution.

trials.hypothesis: The selected 12-byte-advance full-SIMD parent measured 25.32 μs; prior full-SIMD measurements include 13.38 μs, while measured hybrid candidates were slower at roughly 46.94–56.77 μs. This standalone full-SIMD variant advances 16 bytes per vector instead of revalidating four overlap bytes, carrying expected continuations across blocks and using a bounded lookahead byte to SIMD-check restricted second-byte ranges in every lane. It tests the effect of stride and carry handling without combining the hybrid path; no speedup is presumed.

retained: Changed the full-SIMD loop to process 16 new bytes per iteration, using a bounds-checked byte at index+16 for the last lane's second-byte validation.
Classified ASCII, continuation, and legal lead bytes with SSE2 masks; checked continuation relationships with an expected-continuation carry across vector boundaries.
Built the second-byte vector by shifting the loaded block and inserting the bounded lookahead byte, then SIMD-checked the restricted E0, ED, F0, and F4 ranges across all lanes.
Checked any pending continuation bytes before delegating the remaining bounded tail to the strict scalar UTF-8 validator.
Preserved the run ABI, full uint32_t result, input immutability, and serial execution.

trials.hypothesis: A 16-entry high-nibble class lookup and a small scalar continuation-state machine replace per-sequence decoding branches with per-byte classification. The per-byte lookup and state checks may outweigh the reduced lead-byte dispatch, so measure rather than presume a gain. The catalog reports prior byte-class DFA and ASCII-word-skip state-machine variants at 113.39 µs and 73.09 µs, while its best reported direct scalar result is 40.76 µs; this is a contrasting compact-table design, not a SIMD variant.

retained: Replace sequence-length-specific continuation checks with a scalar scan that tracks remaining continuation bytes and the allowed range for the next byte.

Use a 16-entry high-nibble classification table for ASCII, continuation, and lead-byte classes; reject invalid leads, overlong encodings, surrogate encodings, values above U+10FFFF, and incomplete sequences at end of input.
Read only the current byte within the supplied length and preserve the existing ABI, complete uint32 output, read-only input, and serial execution.

trials.hypothesis: The selected full-SIMD parent measured 13.38 μs, while prior hybrid variants measured about 46.94–56.77 μs. This standalone hybrid tests a contrasting detector and fallback: eight bounded 64-bit word checks skip complete ASCII blocks, while any mixed block is decoded with the strict scalar validator through code-point starts before its boundary. Word detection may reduce classification work, but scalar fallback on mixed data may still dominate; no speedup is presumed.

retained: Replace the parent's full-SIMD validator with a separate hybrid path; do not combine the alternatives.
Detect complete 64-byte blocks using eight in-bounds memcpy loads of uint64_t words and a repeated high-bit mask; skip a block only when all bytes are ASCII.
For a mixed block, strictly decode code points starting before its boundary, allowing a valid sequence to cross that boundary and resuming at the first unconsumed byte.
Validate the remaining tail with the same strict scalar decoder, checking continuation bytes, overlong forms, surrogates, out-of-range values, and truncation without reading past n.
Preserve the run ABI, full uint32_t output, input immutability, and serial execution.

trials.hypothesis: Replacing repeated byte-at-a-time ASCII-loop control flow with a bounded four-byte scalar OR check may reduce loop branches for ASCII runs. The four scalar loads, OR, bounds check, and bytewise replay of up to three ASCII bytes in a mixed block may instead add cost, particularly for inputs with frequent multibyte sequences. Prior measurements favor direct scalar parsing (40.76 µs best reported) over the selected parent (48.10 µs), while an 8-byte high-bit scan measured 59.81 µs and a per-byte DFA 76.68 µs; this smaller scalar chunk tests whether reduced chunk overhead changes the tradeoff. No speedup is presumed.

retained: Replace the byte-at-a-time ASCII fast scan with a bounds-checked four-byte scan using scalar byte loads and an OR of their high bits; fall back to the bytewise scan when a block includes a non-ASCII byte.
Retain the existing width derivation, bounded continuation reads, and lead-specific second-byte bounds for complete UTF-8 validation.
Preserve the ABI, uint32 output, read-only input, serial execution, and thread budget.

trials.hypothesis: A full-SIMD validator already has favorable measured results relative to prior hybrid candidates. This variant tests whether quickly accepting a fully ASCII 16-byte vector avoids enough byte-class and range-check work to improve on the measured full-SIMD leader. It still applies SIMD validation to every mixed vector; carry handling prevents an ASCII fast path from hiding a pending continuation. The workload's byte mix and any speedup remain unknown until measured.

retained: Replace the scalar-only scan with a serial 16-byte SSE2 validator that classifies byte classes, checks continuation masks with a cross-block carry, and validates the restricted second-byte ranges for E0, ED, F0, and F4.
Before full vector validation, use the SSE2 sign-bit movemask to accept an all-ASCII vector only when no continuation is pending; update the previous vector and carry consistently for the next block.

Process two ordered vectors per 32-byte outer iteration, then remaining complete vectors; use the strict bounds-checked scalar decoder for the tail and back up to a possible crossing sequence's lead when carry remains.
Keep every vector load within the input length, preserve the run ABI and full uint32_t output, leave input unchanged, and remain serial.

trials.hypothesis: For valid multibyte input, accumulating all continuation and scalar-range failures before one rejection branch per sequence may reduce conditional control flow compared with the current short-circuit chains. The extra predicate accumulation and dependencies may cost more, so measure rather than presume a gain. This avoids SIMD and lookup tables: prior correct T2 variants measured 56.17 µs for a four-byte ASCII check, 59.81 µs for an eight-byte high-bit scan, and 76.68 µs for a byte-class DFA; the baseline measured 49.60 µs, while the catalog's best reported candidate measured 40.76 µs.

retained: Preserve the serial ASCII fast path and direct lead-byte/sequence-length dispatch.
Check the remaining input length before loading any continuation bytes; accumulate continuation and Unicode scalar-value violations with bitwise operations, then branch once per multibyte sequence.
Retain rejection of overlong forms, surrogate encodings, illegal leads, and values above U+10FFFF, while preserving the ABI, uint32 output, read-only input, and thread behavior.

trials.hypothesis: The selected validator performs a high-nibble lookup and class checks for each byte. A table-free scalar continuation-state machine may reduce lookup overhead, although its range branches and state updates could cost more. The measured high-nibble DFA was correct but took 76.68 µs, versus 40.53 µs for a prior correct scalar variant; this experiment tests the lookup-versus-branch tradeoff without SIMD.

retained: Replace the per-byte high-nibble class lookup with scalar lead-byte range dispatch and a continuation-state counter.
Track restricted first-continuation ranges for E0, ED, F0, and F4 to reject overlong encodings, surrogates, and values above U+10FFFF.
Read one byte only after the loop's length check and reject incomplete sequences at end of input; preserve the existing ABI, uint32 output, read-only input, and serial execution.

trials.hypothesis: A compile-time 9-state, 256-byte transition table can replace per-byte sequence-dispatch and continuation branches with one state-dependent lookup plus the scan loop. Its table footprint and serial state dependency may cost more than direct scalar parsing; earlier scalar DFA and table approaches were slower, so this experiment tests the tradeoff without presuming a gain. The generated transitions preserve strict UTF-8 scalar-value bounds and make invalid input an absorbing state; end-of-input is accepted only in the initial state.

retained: Replace direct lead-byte parsing with a compile-time-generated 9-state by 256-byte transition table.
Encode continuation count and the E0, ED, F0, and F4 second-byte restrictions in state transitions; make invalid input absorbing and accept only a complete state at end-of-input.
Scan exactly the supplied length with no overreads, SIMD, input writes, ABI changes, or thread-budget changes.

trials.hypothesis: The selected full-SIMD parent measured 25.32 μs, the best reported full-SIMD candidate measured 13.38 μs, and prior measured hybrid candidates were slower (about 46.94–59.73 μs). This standalone 32-byte hybrid tests whether two bounded SSE2 high-bit-detection loads per ASCII block can skip blocks efficiently, while mixed blocks use strict scalar decoding through code-point starts before the block end. This contrasts with the tested smaller and larger hybrid blocks without presuming a speedup.

retained: Replace the selected full-SIMD validator with a separate hybrid route: scan complete 32-byte blocks using two bounded unaligned SSE2 loads and skip only when their OR has no high bits.
For any mixed block, use a strict scalar UTF-8 decoder through code-point starts before its boundary, permitting validated sequences to cross into the following bytes.
Use the same scalar decoder for the remaining tail, with length checks for truncation and checks for invalid continuations, overlong forms, surrogates, and out-of-range values.
Preserve the run ABI, full uint32_t result, input immutability, serial execution, and no-read-beyond-n behavior.

trials.hypothesis: A reverse scalar scan can collect continuation bytes and validate their count and lead-specific scalar bounds once the lead is reached. This changes the control flow from forward sequence dispatch and length checks to per-byte continuation classification; the added state and branches may outweigh any savings, so performance must be measured.

retained: Replace the forward ASCII/lead-byte parser with a reverse scan that counts continuation bytes and records the earliest continuation in each sequence.
At each lead, require the exact continuation count and enforce the UTF-8 overlong, surrogate, and U+10FFFF boundary restrictions; reject invalid leads, misplaced continuations, and incomplete input.
Read only bytes guarded by the reverse-loop index and preserve the existing ABI, uint32 output, read-only input, and serial execution.

trials.hypothesis: The selected 32-byte-unrolled full-SIMD parent is the measured leader at 13.38 μs. A 64-byte outer unroll may reduce loop-control overhead while preserving its sequential SIMD validation and carry handling; the larger body may instead hurt. Earlier hybrid variants measured substantially slower, so this is a separate full-SIMD experiment, not an additive combination. The outcome must be measured under the unchanged protocol.

retained: Increase the full-SIMD outer unroll from 32 to 64 bytes by validating four ordered 16-byte blocks per full iteration.
Propagate continuation carry and the previous vector sequentially through all four blocks so multibyte sequences crossing vector and outer-block boundaries remain checked.
Retain bounded 32-byte and 16-byte residual loops and the existing strict scalar tail; do not read beyond length.
Preserve the run ABI, complete uint32_t output, input immutability, serial execution, and the existing SSE2 instruction set.

trials.hypothesis: A four-byte scalar-unrolled ASCII probe may reduce loop-control decisions across ASCII runs, while retaining the existing direct scalar sequence checks for non-ASCII bytes. The extra loads and OR, and up to three repeated ASCII-byte checks when a probe block contains a multibyte lead, may offset any gain; the unchanged correctness suite and repeated timing will decide.

retained: Add a four-byte, in-bounds scalar probe that advances over a block only when every byte is ASCII; otherwise fall back to the scalar byte scan at that block.

Retain direct scalar lead-byte dispatch with explicit remaining-length checks and rejection of overlong encodings, surrogates, illegal leads, and values above U+10FFFF; use no SIMD lane validation or lookup table.
Preserve the existing ABI, complete uint32 output, read-only input, and serial execution.

trials.hypothesis: Skipping the remaining SIMD checks when a full 16-byte block is entirely ASCII and no continuation is pending may reduce work on ASCII-rich inputs. The extra branch may instead hurt when most blocks contain non-ASCII bytes; the official mixed-width measurement will decide.

retained: After a bounded 16-byte load, bypass continuation-mask, byte-class, and restricted-range checks when carry is zero and the vector movemask indicates that all lanes are ASCII; update previous and next_carry consistently before returning.
